opus-5.5.text:
I think the difficulty is often misunderstood. People look at embodied intelligence and see a huge, fast-growing market, and they assume that if you make a good motor, a good reducer, a good sensor, or a good dexterous hand, you can just plug into it. But the reality is that the market is still in a very early, very fragmented stage, and that makes being a supplier quite hard.

First, the demand itself is not stable yet. Most robot companies are still iterating on their architectures. One generation might use a certain joint design, and six months later they've changed the degrees of freedom, the torque requirements, or even the whole form factor. So as a supplier, you're chasing a moving target. You invest in tooling, in validation, in a production line, and then the specification shifts. That's very different from the automotive industry, where a platform is locked in for years and you know your volume.

Second, the volumes are still small. Everyone talks about humanoids shipping in the millions someday, but right now, for most customers, an order might be a few hundred or a few thousand units. At that scale, it's very hard to get the cost down, and it's very hard to justify building dedicated capacity. So you end up in a chicken-and-egg situation: the robot makers want lower prices to scale, but you can only lower prices once there's scale.

Third, the technical bar is actually higher than people expect. Components for embodied robots have to be compact, lightweight, high power density, reliable under constant dynamic load, and increasingly they need to be "smart"—with integrated sensing, control, and data feedback. It's not just mechanical precision anymore; you need to understand the control loop and how the model on top will use your hardware. Suppliers who come from traditional industrial automation often underestimate this.

And fourth, there's the question of trust and positioning. Many of the leading robot companies are trying to vertically integrate the core parts because they see those as their moat. So a supplier has to prove that they bring something the customer can't easily do in-house—either a real technical edge, or a cost and manufacturing advantage that's very hard to replicate. If you're just a "me too" supplier, you'll get squeezed.

So my view is: getting into this market is not about having one good product. It's about being patient enough to co-develop with customers through several iterations, being financially able to survive the low-volume period, and having a clear judgment about which parts of the stack will stay outsourced in the long run. The companies that make it through will be the ones that grow together with the industry, rather than waiting for the industry to be ready for them.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think most people underestimate how hard it is, and the reason is that embodied intelligence right now isn't really a market in the traditional sense. It's a lot of very different customers, each with very different needs, and almost none of them have figured out what they actually want.

When you supply components into, say, electric vehicles, there's a reference architecture. Everyone roughly agrees on what a battery pack needs to do, what a motor controller needs to do, what the interfaces look like. You can design a product once and sell it to twenty customers. In humanoids and general-purpose robots today, there's no consensus on anything. Should the hand have five fingers or three? Tendon-driven or direct-drive? Is the joint supposed to be a planetary gearbox, a harmonic drive, a cycloidal reducer? Every team has its own answer, and every answer is still changing quarter by quarter. So as a supplier you're not building a product, you're building a different custom solution for each customer, and you're absorbing the cost of their indecision.

The second difficulty is that your customers themselves don't have volume. A robotics startup might order fifty units, then a hundred, then say they're going to need ten thousand next year, and that ten thousand might never come. If you tool up for that, you're carrying the risk on their behalf. If you don't tool up, you can't hit the cost and performance targets they need to be competitive. So you're constantly deciding how much to believe the roadmap.

The third thing, which I think is less visible from the outside, is that the specifications these companies ask for are often beyond what the supply chain can deliver at any reasonable price. They want the torque density of an aerospace actuator, the cost of a consumer appliance, and the reliability of an industrial robot, all at the same time. And they're not being unreasonable, because that genuinely is what a useful humanoid requires. But it means you're not just manufacturing, you're doing R&D in parallel with your customer, and you have to decide whether you're willing to fund that.

And then there's the question of who captures the value. If you become very good at one component, the big integrators will eventually want to bring it in-house, or they'll second-source you to death. So you have to ask whether you're building a durable position or just a temporary convenience for someone else.

So my honest view is that entering this market as a supplier is less about having the technology and more about having the patience and the balance sheet to survive several years of uncertainty before the architecture settles. The ones who win will probably be those who picked the right handful of customers early, grew with them, and were still standing when the volume finally arrived.

astra-6.text:
I think the difficulty is that you’re entering a market where both the product and the division of labor are still taking shape. As a supplier, you need to know what you can deliver consistently, but you also need customers who know what they need. In embodied intelligence, those requirements can change as the customer tests the system in real environments.

So having a strong component or a good demonstration is only the beginning. You have to show that your technology works inside the customer’s system, that it’s reliable, and that the cost makes sense. That often requires a lot of joint development. The challenge is making sure each project helps you build a repeatable product, rather than becoming a completely separate engineering job.

My view is that the practical entry point is a specific problem with a clear way to measure success. Solve that problem well, earn the customer’s trust, and expand from there. The real barrier is turning technical capability into something customers can confidently build their own products around.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the difficulty is that you’re entering a market where the requirements are still taking shape. As a supplier, you need to know what your customer actually needs, but the customer may still be exploring the product, the application, and even the technical approach. So you’re developing against a moving target.

That makes it difficult to balance customization and standardization. If you customize everything for one customer, you may win a project but struggle to build a repeatable business. If you standardize too early, your product may not solve anyone’s problem well enough.

My view is that you need to start with a concrete application, work closely with customers, and prove that you can deliver reliably. The barrier isn’t just technical performance. It’s whether you can turn that performance into something customers can integrate, afford, and use consistently.
